units.text: Follow the blue connection from the client to the Application Load Balancer. This first TLS connection terminates at the load balancer, which presents its server certificate.
Follow the yellow connection next. An HTTPS target group creates a separate TLS connection from the load balancer to the target, using the certificate installed on that target.
Compare the dashed lower path. With an HTTP target group, the backend connection is unencrypted, even when the client used HTTPS.

The target certificate supports encryption on this second leg. An Application Load Balancer does not validate the target certificate, so this is not the same certificate-validation boundary as the client connection.
Return to the complete picture. There are two independent connections. Choose an HTTPS target group when encryption must continue from the load balancer to the target.
Start with the left side. The load balancer presents its server certificate, and the client validates it during the TLS handshake.
Follow the lower arrow toward the load balancer. Mutual TLS also asks the client to prove its identity with a certificate and the corresponding private key.
The upper branch is verify mode. The load balancer checks the client certificate against its configured trust store. Certificate revocation lists can provide optional revocation checks.
The lower branch is passthrough mode. The load balancer forwards the client certificate chain in HTTP headers, and the application must validate it. This is not transparent TCP passthrough.
Read the footer with both modes visible. Certificate authentication establishes identity. The application still decides which actions that identity is authorized to perform.
Begin with issue and deploy on the left. Check the domain name, the certificate chain, and the endpoint and Region where the certificate is installed.
Move to renewal on the right. Monitor expiry and maintain required validation records. An imported ACM certificate must be replaced through your own renewal process.
The lower panel covers revocation. Use the revocation mechanisms supported by the actual client or service. A revocation record is useful only when the relying party checks it.
Follow the troubleshooting strip: hostname, trust chain, validity dates, and endpoint configuration. Treat these as separate checks so a certificate problem does not become a guessing exercise.

Review the complete lifecycle. Issue and deploy correctly, renew before expiry, and test how clients respond to revoked certificates. Changes to a trust anchor can affect many certificates, so assess that scope before updating a trust store.
